claims.text: The corrosion resistance of steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications is primarily governed by a dense Cr2O3 surface passivation film.
A chromium content of at least 10% is required for the proposed corrosion-resistance mechanism.
Exposure at 20-100°C and 40-80% humidity under a constant flow of corrosive species will produce a dense Cr2O3 passivation film.
Dense Cr2O3 passivation films form on the surfaces of stainless steels and Fe-Cr alloys.
The Cr2O3 film prevents penetration of corrosive species by acting as a physical or chemical barrier.
A Cr-rich or Cr2O3-containing passivation film reduces the corrosion rate of stainless steel.
Steel possessing a Cr2O3 passivation film will have a corrosion rate at least 50% lower than steel without such a film.
The mechanism remains valid throughout 20-100°C and 40-80% humidity for all steels containing at least 10% chromium.
Other alloying elements or oxide layers may also contribute to corrosion resistance.
Microstructural factors can alter corrosion resistance through changes in chromium enrichment of the passivation film.
The hypothesis can be tested by exposing steels with different chromium contents to a controlled corrosive environment and measuring their corrosion rates.
Steel without a Cr2O3 passivation film serves as the baseline control.
The hypothesis is falsified if steels containing at least 10% chromium do not show a corrosion-rate reduction of at least 50% relative to steels without a Cr2O3 film.
